title: Module 1: Devices and Signals
text:
Learning Goals

Read in accelerometry data
describe the signals produced by a tri-axial accelerometer;
identify the device families used by major cohort studies.

title: Module 1: Devices and Signals
text:
Slide: The Device Landscape
Commercial wearables, such as watches and fitness trackers, are designed around a consumer experience. They often expose proprietary step, sleep, or activity scores, while the raw signal and processing rules may be unavailable or change over time.
Research-grade accelerometers are configured for a study protocol. They retain high-frequency raw acceleration and device metadata, making calibration, quality control, and alternative processing choices possible. The trade-off is that the analyst, rather than a vendor, must make and document the processing decisions.









Device class
Typical output
Strength
Limitation




Commercial wearable
Proprietary summaries, sometimes raw data
Low participant burden
Vendor algorithms can be opaque


Research-grade accelerometer
Raw time, x, y, z, and metadata
Transparent, reproducible processing
Requires a full analysis pipeline

title: Module 1: Devices and Signals
text:
Devices in Large Studies
ActiGraph GT3X and GT9X devices are commonly used in United States cohort studies, including NHATS, NHANES, and ARIC. They are tri-axial accelerometers and are often encountered as .gt3x archives.
Axivity AX3 devices are compact, research-grade accelerometers that store data in .cwa files. The UK Biobank accelerometry study used AX3 devices at the wrist. The device is not the study: placement, wear protocol, sampling frequency, dynamic range, and processing rules jointly define the measurement.

title: Module 1: Devices and Signals
text:
What Is Measured?
At each sample, a tri-axial accelerometer records acceleration along three device-fixed axes. The observed vector combines gravity, movement, orientation, sensor noise, and any remaining calibration error. It does not directly observe steps, sleep, sedentary behavior, or intensity.
The raw signal is often expressed in gravitational units (g), where stationary data should have vector magnitude close to 1 g after calibration. Device axes rotate with the device, so a change in x, y, or z alone need not indicate a change in behavior.

title: Module 1: Devices and Signals
text:
The Measurement Is a Protocol
The same activity can produce different signals at the wrist, hip, thigh, or waist. Wrist data are often noisier because normal arm movement contributes acceleration; algorithms developed for hip placement, especially legacy step and count algorithms, may not transfer to the wrist.
Before collection, specify the body location, dominant or non-dominant wrist, device orientation if relevant, dynamic range, sampling frequency, wear schedule, and whether other sensors (for example, temperature or light) are available. These are measurement decisions, not administrative details.

title: Module 1: Devices and Signals
text:
Raw Data Preserve Choices
Raw sub-second acceleration in g is the most portable starting point because it retains the signal needed to apply or compare processing methods later. Proprietary daily activity, step, or sleep scores can be useful endpoints, but their algorithms may be opaque and can change with firmware or software updates.
The course therefore treats vendor summaries as a documented input or comparator—not as a substitute for the raw signal and processing record.

title: Module 1: Devices and Signals
text:
Preparation for the Next Module
The course data directory contains one file from each device family:

data/TAS1H30182791 (2026-04-29).gt3x: an ActiGraph GT3X archive;
data/114890_0000000000.cwa: an Axivity AX3 file.

The next module turns these device files into the common raw-data representation: a timestamp and three acceleration columns.

Schoenborn, Charlotte A., and Manfred Stommel. 2011. “Adherence to the 2008 Adult Physical Activity Guidelines and Mortality Risk.” American Journal of Preventive Medicine 40 (5): 514–21. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amepre.2010.12.029.

title: Module 6: Valid Days
text:
From Minutes to Valid Days
First classify each minute as wear or non-wear. Then calculate daily wear time and apply a prespecified threshold, such as at least 10 hours of waking wear time. A valid-day indicator is an analytic eligibility flag, not a claim that the day is complete or representative.
The calendar day must be constructed in the declared analysis timezone. Daylight-saving transitions are not always 1,440 minutes long, and a midnight boundary may not be appropriate for a sleep-centered outcome. Define the day window before calculating wear time.

title: Module 6: Valid Days
text:
Counts Are Common, Not Required
Choi and Troiano procedures require activity counts and thus fit naturally in count-based studies. Raw-signal methods can determine non-wear without counts, for example using acceleration variability, temperature, or a model-based detector. The inclusion rule should describe the signal used to infer wear, not simply label an interval as “valid.”
Many established protocols still use counts at least for non-wear detection even when the primary outcome is ENMO, MIMS, or another raw-derived measure. That hybrid design is defensible when it is intentional and documented; it should not happen by accident because a default function was used.

title: Module 6: Valid Days
text:
Report the Attrition
At minimum, report days observed, days with sufficient wear, days excluded for non-wear, and the participant-level rule that follows. Stratify these quantities when missingness could be related to the population or outcome of interest.

title: Module 6: Valid Days
section: Missing Data Are Not Automatically Imputable
text:
Missing Data Are Not Automatically Imputable
Do not fill non-wear or missing minutes with a participant’s average activity simply to create a complete day. Such imputation changes the estimand and can hide informative missingness. First report the observed-data estimand; then use a separate, justified imputation or sensitivity analysis if the scientific question requires a complete profile.

title: wearabler
text:
Wearabler Course Outline
This site is set up as a Quarto-based short course on accelerometry and wearable data analysis.
The module structure follows the shared course-planning chat and is organized around the activerse packages:

actibase
actiread
actimetrics
asleep
walking
stepcount

Start with the module index.

title: Module 2: Import and Structure
text:
Core Representation
Raw accelerometry is, at its core, a time series with four essential columns:







Column
Meaning




time
A datetime timestamp identifying when the sample was recorded


x
Acceleration along the device x axis


y
Acceleration along the device y axis


z
Acceleration along the device z axis



The timestamp is not merely a row number. Its timezone, precision, regularity, and gaps determine day boundaries, sleep windows, wear-time intervals, and the validity of all downstream summaries. The x, y, and z columns are the core of raw accelerometry; device headers and processing history are essential accompanying metadata.

title: Module 2: Import and Structure
section: Read the Local Files with actiread
text:
Read the Local Files with actiread
actiread provides a common R-facing import layer for the two file types used in this course. Import first, inspect second, and standardize before calculating a metric.

library(actibase)
library(actiread)

gt3x_file <- "data/TAS1H30182791 (2026-04-29).gt3x"
cwa_file <- "data/114890_0000000000.cwa"

gt3x_raw <- acti_read_gt3x(gt3x_file, verbose = FALSE)
cwa_raw <- acti_read_cwa(cwa_file, verbose = FALSE)

gt3x <- acti_standardize_data(gt3x_raw)
cwa <- acti_standardize_data(cwa_raw)

head(gt3x[, c("time", "x", "y", "z")])
attributes(gt3x)

Before proceeding, verify the timezone, sampling frequency, acceleration units, start and end times, duplicate timestamps, and gaps. Preserve the original file and keep import metadata with the derived table.

title: Module 2: Import and Structure
text:
Timestamps Need Their Own QC
Sub-second algorithms depend on fractional seconds. Display enough precision to see them (for example, options(digits.secs = 3)) and check observed intervals rather than assuming that every nominal 80 Hz file is exactly 80 Hz at every timestamp. Rounding milliseconds during a CSV export can corrupt joins, inferred sampling rates, resampling, and step algorithms.
Use an explicit timezone. UTC avoids daylight-saving discontinuities during processing, while local time is often needed for sleep windows, diary linkage, and calendar-day summaries. Record the original timezone, the analysis timezone, and every conversion between them.

raw |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    duplicate_times = sum(duplicated(time)),
    smallest_interval_s = min(diff(as.numeric(time))),
    largest_interval_s = max(diff(as.numeric(time)))
  )

title: Module 2: Import and Structure
section: Missing Samples Are Not Zero Movement
text:
Missing Samples Are Not Zero Movement
An ActiGraph may enter idle sleep mode and create an all-zero segment. A gap can also reflect charging, export, or reader behavior. Neither condition proves that the participant was inactive or that the device was not worn.
Keep a flag for imputed, inserted, or altered samples. Do not silently fill a gap with zeroes before calibration or metric calculation: zero-filled segments can distort gravity correction, non-wear detection, and activity summaries. Inspect a short plot of each imported file before standardizing it.

title: Module 2: Import and Structure
section: Read the Axivity File with GGIRread
text:
Read the Axivity File with GGIRread
GGIRread is a useful independent reader for Axivity .cwa data. Its output needs to be converted to the course’s common time, x, y, z convention before it can be compared with another reader.

ax3 <- GGIRread::readAxivity(
  filename = "data/114890_0000000000.cwa",
  desiredtz = "America/New_York"
)

str(ax3)
# Extract the time and x/y/z components, then rename them to the common schema.

title: Module 2: Import and Structure
section: Read the Axivity File with Python actipy
text:
Read the Axivity File with Python actipy
reticulate lets an R analysis call Python’s actipy without leaving the project. This is especially helpful for comparing reader and preprocessing implementations. Set processing options explicitly; do not silently accept defaults as a study protocol.

library(reticulate)

actipy <- import("actipy")
result <- actipy$read_device(
  "data/114890_0000000000.cwa",
  lowpass_hz = 20,
  calibrate_gravity = TRUE,
  detect_nonwear = FALSE,
  resample_hz = 50
)

ax3_py <- py_to_r(result[[1]])
ax3_info <- py_to_r(result[[2]])
head(ax3_py)
ax3_info[c("SampleRate", "CalibErrorBefore(mg)", "CalibErrorAfter(mg)")]

title: Module 2: Import and Structure
text:
Learning Check
Can you state the sampling frequency and timezone for each imported file, and can you create a four-column table named time, x, y, and z without changing the raw values? If not, the import step is not complete.

title: Module 3: Calibration
text:
Why Calibrate?
An ideal stationary device has a vector magnitude of 1 g, regardless of orientation. Real sensors have axis-specific offset, scale, and temperature-related error. Calibration estimates a transformation so the recorded signal is closer to this physical reference.
Calibration is not an optional cosmetic cleanup. A small offset can change low-intensity metrics, sedentary thresholds, and non-wear decisions, especially when comparing devices or participants.

title: Module 3: Calibration
text:
Calibration Philosophy
The aim is not to force every recording to look alike. The aim is to correct identifiable sensor error while preserving genuine movement. A good workflow retains the uncalibrated data, records the estimated correction and diagnostics, applies the same rule across the study, and flags files whose calibration cannot be supported by the observed data.
Calibration should be evaluated before and after correction. If the data never include sufficiently varied stationary orientations, an autocalibration routine may be poorly identified; that uncertainty belongs in the QC record rather than being hidden.

title: Module 3: Calibration
text:
Raw-Signal Quality Checks Come First
Calibration cannot repair every problem. Inspect the raw signal for duplicate or irregular times, long gaps, all-zero runs, clipped values at the device’s acceleration limit, isolated extreme spikes, and implausibly constant axes. A recorded value near the configured limit can be real, but repeated saturation should be flagged because it limits what a metric can recover.
Do this assessment before calibration. In particular, a zero-filled idle-sleep segment does not represent a stationary device on the unit sphere and can bias an autocalibration fit. Preserve an event flag and decide explicitly whether each affected segment is excluded, repaired, or retained.

title: Module 3: Calibration
text:
Common Approaches








Approach
Idea
Main consideration




Factory calibration
Use manufacturer sensor settings
May not address drift or deployment-specific error


Static reference check
Compare a stationary device to 1 g
Requires a controlled reference period


Autocalibration
Estimate offset and scale from repeated stationary orientations in free-living data
Needs enough orientation diversity and a QC threshold


Cross-device harmonization
Relate outputs from different devices or pipelines
Does not replace sensor-level calibration



actipy exposes gravity calibration while it reads a file; its diagnostics report calibration error before and after processing. The same principle applies regardless of software: inspect the diagnostic, record the choice, and do not treat a failed calibration as silently corrected.

library(reticulate)
actipy <- import("actipy")

result <- actipy$read_device(
  "data/114890_0000000000.cwa",
  calibrate_gravity = TRUE,
  detect_nonwear = FALSE
)
info <- py_to_r(result[[2]])
info[c("CalibErrorBefore(mg)", "CalibErrorAfter(mg)", "CalibOK")]

title: Module 3: Calibration
Module 3: Calibration
text:
Calibration Is Not Harmonization
Correcting sensor offset and scale does not make wrist and hip data equivalent, nor does it make two different metric definitions interchangeable. If a study changes device, sampling rate, placement, or processing software, evaluate comparability with a planned bridge or sensitivity analysis. Retain the uncalibrated signal so that a revised calibration rule can be applied later.
The following module derives signal metrics from these explicitly defined inputs.

title: Module 4: Signal Metrics
section: From Vectors to a Signal Metric
text:
From Vectors to a Signal Metric
Let the calibrated acceleration vector at a sample be (x, y, z), measured in g, with vector magnitude VM = sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2). A metric turns a stream of vectors into an epoch-level quantity. Metric selection is a scientific and compatibility decision, not a purely technical one.








Metric
Definition
Interpretation




ENMO
mean(max(VM - 1 g, 0)) within an epoch
Dynamic acceleration above gravity, commonly expressed in mg


MAD
mean(abs(VM - mean(VM))) within an epoch
Within-epoch variation in vector magnitude


MIMS
A monitor-independent movement summary after filtering and integration
Designed to be interpretable across monitor settings


Activity counts
Device-algorithm output after proprietary-style filtering, thresholding, and integration
Legacy outcome used in many surveillance and cohort protocols



Other useful summaries include the activity index (variation relative to a resting-noise reference), area under the acceleration curve (AUC), and step counts. They answer different questions and carry their own assumptions; none is a universal definition of physical activity.

title: Module 4: Signal Metrics
text:
Activity Counts Still Matter
Activity counts are not raw acceleration. They depend on a specific transformation and therefore cannot be recreated perfectly from arbitrary raw data without knowing the count algorithm and device configuration. Yet counts remain central to historic protocols, published thresholds, and some non-wear algorithms.
MIMS was developed as a monitor-independent summary and has shown close correspondence with ActiGraph activity counts in validation work. That association makes MIMS useful when bridging count-based literature and raw-signal workflows, but it does not make the two metrics interchangeable. Compare them at the same epoch length, placement, preprocessing configuration, and target population.

title: Module 4: Signal Metrics
text:
Compare Metrics on One Segment
Use one calibrated segment and a fixed epoch length. Plot each metric on its own scale, inspect rank ordering and transition periods, and report the processing steps that produced it.

# Pseudocode: use the same standardized, calibrated raw table for every metric.
# metrics_5s <- raw |>
#   group_by(epoch = floor_date(time, "5 seconds")) |>
#   summarise(enmo_mg = ..., mad_mg = ..., mims = ..., counts = ...)
#
# plot(metrics_5s$epoch, metrics_5s$enmo_mg, type = "l")

title: Module 4: Signal Metrics
text:
Learning Check
For every metric, can you state its input units, epoch length, calibration status, filtering rules, and whether it is intended to reproduce a legacy count-based outcome? Those choices belong in the method, not only in code.

title: Module 4: Signal Metrics
section: Resampling and Filtering Are Decisions, Not Defaults
text:
Resampling and Filtering Are Decisions, Not Defaults
Most metrics do not require resampling merely because a device has a different native rate. Resample only when an algorithm requires a particular rate, when rates differ within the analysis, or when a justified signal-processing objective requires it. Interpolation changes the data and should be marked in provenance.
Filtering can remove sensor noise or isolate a frequency range, but it can also alter peaks, transitions, and count-like metrics. Record filter type, cutoff frequencies, order, implementation, and whether filtering occurred before or after calibration. Choose the processing path for the target metric rather than applying one generic preprocessing recipe.

title: Module 5: Wear and Seven-Day Visualization
text:
Wear Is an Inference Problem
Non-wear is not directly observed by the accelerometer. It is inferred from sustained low movement, sometimes together with temperature or other device signals. The rule affects both which minutes enter a summary and which days qualify for inclusion.
Two common count-based rules are:







Rule
Core idea




Troiano
A long run of zero counts, allowing a limited interruption of low counts under prespecified rules


Choi
A sustained zero-count window with a spike-tolerance rule that is generally more conservative about classifying wear



These are protocol definitions, not universal truths. Both were developed around activity counts. Raw-acceleration pipelines can use alternative non-wear detectors, but count-based Choi or Troiano rules remain important when reproducing legacy analysis plans.

title: Module 5: Wear and Seven-Day Visualization
section: Do Not Confuse Non-wear, Sleep, and Inactivity
text:
Do Not Confuse Non-wear, Sleep, and Inactivity
Low acceleration may mean the device was removed, the participant was asleep, seated, ill, or simply still. Non-wear algorithms estimate device status; sleep algorithms estimate a behavioral state. Treating every quiet interval as non-wear inflates activity, while treating every quiet interval as sleep or wear can underestimate it.
Use diaries and auxiliary sensors when available, but do not assume that they are a gold standard. Compare inferred intervals with the full-week profile and state whether the protocol targets waking wear, 24-hour wear, or a sleep-specific window.

title: Module 5: Wear and Seven-Day Visualization
text:
Aggregate Flags Deliberately
A non-wear flag often starts at the sample or second level but is applied to minute and day summaries. Define the aggregation rule: for example, whether a minute is non-wear if all samples, most samples, or any part of the minute is non-wear. Boundary choices can change eligible minutes and valid-day status.

title: Module 5: Wear and Seven-Day Visualization
text:
Plot a Participant’s Full Week
Represent the week as 10,080 consecutive one-minute observations. A useful plot shows the chosen activity metric over time, adds day boundaries, and shades non-wear intervals. This makes data loss, device removal, and implausible patterns visible before a validity rule hides them in a summary.

# minute_data has: participant_id, time, enmo_mg, wear
# It should contain exactly 7 * 1440 rows for a complete minute-level week.

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(minute_data, aes(time, enmo_mg)) +
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = nonwear$start, xmax = nonwear$end,
    ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
    fill = "grey70", alpha = 0.45
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.2) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "ENMO (mg)",
    title = "Seven-day accelerometry profile",
    subtitle = "Grey shading denotes inferred non-wear"
  )

The plot is a QC artifact: retain it or a comparable diagnostic for each participant or batch, alongside the exact wear algorithm and parameter values.

title: Module 7: Daily and Participant-Level Summaries
Module 7: Daily and Participant-Level Summaries
Module 7: Daily and Participant-Level Summaries
text:
Build an Analysis-Ready Denominator
Carry wear_minutes, available days, valid days, weekend/weekday status, and season with the participant outcome. A single activity value without these variables cannot reveal whether a low value reflects behavior, limited observation, or a protocol decision. For a 24-hour profile, retain the minute-level denominator rather than forcing every profile to be complete.

title: Module 7: Daily and Participant-Level Summaries
text:
Learning Check
State whether your final value estimates an average minute, an average observed day, or an average participant. These are different quantities.

title: Module 8: Downstream and Functional Analysis
text:
Analysis of Participant Summaries
With one outcome per participant, conventional regression can relate average daily activity, sleep, steps, or another summary to exposures and covariates. The model should name the estimand and account for factors that shaped the outcome: device, placement, season, valid-day rule, and the number of usable days.

fit <- lm(mean_daily_enmo_mg ~ age + sex + season + device_model,
          data = participant)
summary(fit)

Participant summaries are compact and interpretable, but they discard timing. Two participants can have the same average daily ENMO while one moves in short morning bouts and the other is active for a long afternoon period.
Processing uncertainty is part of the analysis. Repeat key models under credible alternatives for calibration, non-wear detection, valid-day thresholds, epoch length, or metric definition when conclusions could depend on them. Do not pool outcomes across device placements or metric definitions without establishing what the pooled value represents.

title: Module 8: Downstream and Functional Analysis
text:
Functional Analysis
Functional approaches preserve the shape of an activity profile. Align each participant’s minute-level series to a common clock, smooth or otherwise represent the curve, and model functions, functional principal components, or time-varying associations.
The essential design choices are day alignment, treatment of non-wear, weekday/weekend handling, smoothing basis, and the estimand. Functional analysis does not remove the need for wear QC; it makes inconsistent time alignment more consequential.
Functional profiles also require an explicit missing-data strategy. Mark unobserved clock times, avoid interpreting imputed segments as measured behavior, and distinguish a curve estimated from repeated observed days from a literal complete-day trace. The appropriate method depends on whether timing, total volume, or both are the scientific target.

title: Module 8: Downstream and Functional Analysis
section: Match the Analysis to the Data Product
text:
Match the Analysis to the Data Product







Data product
Example analysis




Valid participant-days
Mixed model or within-person comparison


Participant average across valid days
Cross-sectional regression


24-hour profile
Functional regression or functional PCA


Seven-day profile
Repeated functional or multilevel time-series analysis



The processing pipeline determines what can reasonably be interpreted in each model. Keep the link from a model outcome back to the minute-level definition and QC rules.

title: Module 9: Reproducibility, QC, and Other Methods
section: A Pipeline That Can Be Audited
text:
A Pipeline That Can Be Audited
An auditable project separates immutable raw files, standardized raw tables, calibration diagnostics, minute-level metrics, wear flags, day-level summaries, participant outcomes, and model outputs. Every derived object should retain identifiers, time zone, processing version, and the parameters that created it.
The minimum QC record includes import diagnostics, sampling frequency, calibration status, time gaps, non-wear intervals, valid-day counts, and participant exclusions. Seven-day wear-shaded plots are particularly effective for checking that these rules match the data.
The processing pipeline should also preserve an explicit row-level or interval-level status: observed raw data, inserted/zero-filled sample, excluded artifact, calibrated value, resampled value, and non-wear classification. This makes it possible to trace a final summary back to the original signal without treating altered data as observed data.

title: Module 9: Reproducibility, QC, and Other Methods
Module 9: Reproducibility, QC, and Other Methods
text:
A Practical Pipeline Contract
Each stage should have a declared input, output, and QC check:








Stage
Output
Essential check




Import
Raw time/x/y/z plus metadata
units, timezone, sampling intervals, gaps


Raw QC
Flagged signal
zero runs, clipping, spikes, duplicate times


Calibration
Corrected signal plus diagnostics
before/after error and calibration eligibility


Metric and epoching
Second- or minute-level values
metric units, filtering, epoch rule


Wear and validity
Eligible intervals and days
algorithm parameters and attrition


Analysis
Participant summaries or profiles
estimand and sensitivity analyses



This contract makes implementation differences across R, Python, vendor, and open-source tools visible rather than accidental.

title: Module 9: Reproducibility, QC, and Other Methods
text:
Other Methods Through reticulate
Some specialized accelerometry methods are implemented in Python. reticulate allows an R/Quarto course project to call them while preserving a single documented workflow.







Package
Typical role




stepcount
Step detection and step-based summaries from raw acceleration


actinet
Activity-pattern or behavior-oriented processing workflows


asleep
Sleep inference and sleep-related outputs




library(reticulate)

# Use a project-pinned Python environment, then import the needed method.
stepcount <- import("stepcount")
actinet <- import("actinet")
asleep <- import("asleep")

The R/Python boundary is itself a QC boundary. Record package versions, the interpreter selected by reticulate, input units, sampling frequency, and the exact conversion from R data frames to Python objects. Specialized outputs should enter the same wear, valid-day, and participant-summary framework used for the core acceleration metrics.

title: Module 1: Devices and Signals
text:
What is Raw Accelerometer Data?

Sensor that measures acceleration in 3D space: X/Y/Z
Typically measured in g-forces (g, \(g=9.81m/s^2\)) or m/s²
Sampled at regular(ish) time intervals (e.g., 30Hz, 100Hz)

Timestamp                  X        Y        Z
2025-02-17 12:00:00.0125   0.02     0.98     0.03
2025-02-17 12:00:00.0250   0.04     0.95     0.05
2025-02-17 12:00:00.0375  -0.01     0.99     0.02

title: Module 1: Devices and Signals
text:
Wrist-Worn vs. Hip-Worn Accelerometers








Feature
Wrist-Worn Devices
Hip-Worn Devices




Placement
Worn on wrist
Attached to belt


Compliance

title: Module 1: Devices and Signals
text:
Data Resolution

Raw Accelerometer Data (high-resolution time-series data)

20-100+ samples/second (Hz)

title: Module 1: Devices and Signals

title: Module 1: Devices and Signals
text:
What are the units?

Some times in m/s\(^2\)
Most times in gravitational units (g), 1\(g=9.81m/s^2\)
Stationary data should have vector magnitude close to 1g after calibration.
Axes rotate, so a change in x, y, or z alone may not indicate a change in behavior.

title: Module 2: Reading and Processing Data
text:
Timestamps Need Their Own QC
The timestamp is not merely a row number.

Its timezone, precision, regularity, and gaps determine day boundaries, sleep windows, wear-time intervals, and the validity of all downstream summaries.
Sub-second algorithms depend on fractional seconds. Display enough precision to see them (for example, options(digits.secs = 3)) and check observed intervals rather than assuming that every nominal 80 Hz file is exactly 80 Hz at every timestamp.
Rounding milliseconds during a CSV export can corrupt joins, inferred sampling rates, resampling, and step algorithms.

title: Module 2: Reading and Processing Data
text:
Timestamps Need Their Own QC

Use an explicit timezone.
UTC avoids daylight-saving discontinuities during processing
Local time is often needed for sleep windows, diary linkage, and calendar-day summaries.
Record the original timezone, the analysis timezone, and every conversion between them.
Before proceeding, verify the timezone, sampling frequency, acceleration units, start and end times, duplicate timestamps, and gaps. Preserve the original file and keep import metadata with the derived table.
